stops.teaser: The oldest federal building in the Pacific Northwest, nearly torn down for parking.

story: Pioneer Courthouse is a federal courthouse in Portland. Construction began in 1869, and it is the oldest federal building in the Pacific Northwest and the second-oldest west of the Mississippi River. It was built in stages between 1869 and 1903. Judge Matthew Deady first used it in 1875, when it was called the United States Building.

People also call it the Pioneer Post Office, because a popular downtown post office was inside until 2005. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1973 and became a National Historic Landmark in 1977.

It has survived several attempts to demolish it. In March 1933 city engineer Olaf Laurgaard proposed tearing it down for a parking garage. Architect A. E. Doyle and other local groups sharply opposed the idea, and the building stayed. Today it is one of four main places where the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals hears oral arguments.
stops.fact: The post office inside stayed open until 2005.
stops.disputed: Many people think old buildings are protected automatically. Wikipedia says this one survived several attempts to demolish it.

claims.t: Pioneer Courthouse is the oldest federal building in the Pacific Northwest.
claims.why: Wikipedia: it is the oldest federal building in the Pacific Northwest.

claims.t: Nobody ever tried to tear the courthouse down.
claims.why: Wikipedia says it survived several demolition attempts, including a 1933 proposal.

spot.q: In March 1933 the city engineer proposed tearing the courthouse down. For what?
spot.why: City engineer Olaf Laurgaard proposed tearing it down for a parking garage. Architect A. E. Doyle and local groups opposed the idea, and the building stayed.

story: Portland City Hall is the home of the city's government, and the Italian Renaissance-style building was completed in 1895. It sits on a whole city block along Fourth and Fifth Avenues. The original building cost $600,000. A big renovation in 1996 to 1998 cost $29 million.

The city bought the block in 1890. Henry J. Hefty designed a huge, showy building that looked like the Kremlin, and construction began in 1892. People did not like it, so the new City Hall Commission cancelled the contract and tore out the basement and first floor at a cost of $125,000.

The city then hired the firm of Whidden and Lewis, who were in town for the Portland Hotel project. Their design is the City Hall you see today. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1974.
stops.fact: The first basement was torn out and redone.
stops.disputed: Many people think the first design is always the one that gets built. Wikipedia says this one was thrown out after the foundation was built.

claims.t: Portland City Hall was completed in 1895.
The first design was built exactly as planned.
claims.why: Wikipedia says the contract was cancelled and the work torn out.

spot.q: The first City Hall design was cancelled and torn out. What did people say it looked like?
spot.why: Henry J. Hefty's showy design looked like the Kremlin. People did not like it, so the contract was cancelled and Whidden and Lewis designed the City Hall you see today.

story: Skidmore Fountain was dedicated on September 22, 1888. It honors Stephen G. Skidmore, a wealthy Portland druggist who died in 1883. His will helped pay for it. Sculptor Olin Levi Warner designed it for $18,000, all of which was donated.

It was styled after fountains Skidmore saw at Versailles during his visit to the 1878 Paris Exposition, and it was meant for horses, men and dogs to drink from. At the dedication, Henry Weinhard offered to pump beer into it.
It is Portland's oldest piece of public art, and it gives its name to the Skidmore/Old Town Historic District. It was restored in 2005.

stops.disputed: Many people think a fountain is only for looks. Wikipedia says this one was built for drinking, for horses, men and dogs.

spot.q: Skidmore Fountain was dedicated in 1888. Who was it meant to give a drink to?
spot.why: It was meant for horses, men and dogs to drink from. At the dedication, Henry Weinhard offered to pump beer into it.

stops.clue: Go to Union Station near the west bank of the Willamette River in Old Town Chinatown. Look for a red-roofed brick station with a tall clock tower.

story: Portland Union Station opened on February 14, 1896. The first design, from McKim, Mead & White in 1882, would have been the largest train station in the world. A smaller plan by Van Brunt & Howe was accepted in 1885, and construction began in 1890. It cost $300,000.

The station has bright red metal roof tiles, red pressed brick and gray sandstone trim. Its signature piece is the 150-foot Romanesque Revival clock tower. The four-sided Seth Thomas clock dates to 1898. Each face is 12 feet across, and the clock has a 14-foot pendulum and a counterweight of about 1,000 pounds that drops almost 50 feet in a week.

The clock is wound every seven days. Neon signs reading Go by Train were added to the tower in 1948. The station joined the National Register of Historic Places in 1975, and Amtrak trains still stop there.
stops.fact: The clock is wound by hand every seven days.
stops.disputed: Many people think big station clocks run on electricity. Wikipedia says this one has a pendulum and a counterweight that has to be wound every seven days.

claims.why: Wikipedia says it has a pendulum and a weight, and it is wound every seven days.

spot.q: The postcard shows the station's clock tower. How often is its Seth Thomas clock wound?
spot.why: The clock is wound every seven days. Its counterweight of about 1,000 pounds drops almost 50 feet in a week.
